Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we're going to learn about avalanche breakdown and Zener breakdown.

Key details

  • Before that, we'll go for refreshing of the last topic, comparison of the diode characteristics of germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide.
  • We see that there are different voltages at which the different semiconductor device has different conducting voltages and with respect to forward bias and reverse bias.
  • In the forward bias, we see the germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide, which conduct at different voltages.
  • The reverse bias also, the breakdown also occurs at different voltages.
  • The first is avalanche breakdown for a normal diode we look at.
  • The forward bias region is this, the reverse bias region is this.
  • So in the reverse bias condition, as the voltage increases, the free charge carriers obtain velocity and associated kinetic energy and release additional carriers through collision with the other atomic structure.
  • Hence, the covalent bonds are broken and electron-hole pair are generated.
  • This electron will hit to the walls of an atom, as we see here, and acquire a energy from applied voltage.
  • This will hit based on the energy acquired from applied voltage and produce more and more free electrons.
  • This free electron again will hit the another atoms, and this cumulative process is called avalanche multiplication or ionization process.
  • The Zener breakdown occurs when both P and N-type materials are heavily doped in a semiconductor diode, hence depletion region is narrowed down, as we see from the diagram here.
  • When a small reverse voltage is applied across the diode, a very strong electric field is produced.
  • Due to this electric field, covalent bonds breaks and produce a large number of free charge carriers.
  • So coming to the comparison between the Zener breakdown and avalanche breakdown, first we start with Zener, and on the right-hand side we have avalanche.
  • The first point is, the process in which the electron move across a barrier from valence band of the p-type material to the conduction band of n-type material is known as breakdown voltage, whereas the process of applying a high voltage and increasing the free electron.
  • Coming to the second point, this is observed in a.
  • Zener diode having a Zener breakdown, which varies from five to eight volts, whereas in the case of an avalanche breakdown, this is observed in the normal diode having a voltage greater than the eight volts.
  • Number three, the valence electrons are pulled out into a conduction due to the high electric field in the narrow depletion region.
  • Here, the valence electrons are pushed to the conduction due to the energy imparted with the accelerated electron which gain their velocity due to the collision with other atom.
  • Coming to the fourth point, the increase in temperature decreases with the breakdown voltage.
  • The increase in temperature will increase the breakdown voltage here.
  • The VI characteristics of Zener diode breakdown has sharp value.
  • The VI characteristics of avalanche breakdown is not sharp as.
  • Zener breakdown, as we see from the diagram.
  • Then in the Zener, it occurs in diode that are lightly doped.
  • The effect of variation in the temperature across the semiconductor diode is observed in both forward as well as the reverse characteristics.
  • The rise in temperature generates more electron-hole pair, thus conductivity increases and thus increase in the current.
  • The PN junction diode parameter like reverse saturation current, bias current, reverse breakdown voltage, and barrier voltage are dependent on the temperature.
  • Increase in temperature increases the carrier concentration.
  • As a result, the knee voltage decreases, breakdown voltage increases, while the reverse saturation current also increases.
  • This we can understand with the help of a forward bias and a reverse.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let us also consider the effect of temperature on VI characteristics of the diode.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

Under reverse bias, the change in the temperature across the diode, the reverse saturation current of the diode increases with increase in temperature.

Key details

  • That is, there is a rise of 7% for every degree rise in temperature for both germanium and silicon, and approximately doubles for every 10 degree rise in the temperature.
  • The reverse breakdown voltage, VR, also increases with the temperature increase.
  • Starting from right to the left, initially we have -75 degree centigrade, where the cut-in voltage is at this point.
  • It may be around 0.1 or even less than 0.1.
  • Whereas at 125 degree, the breakdown voltage is increasing, and reverse saturation current also doubles for every 10 degree rise in the temperature.
  • Determine the value if the temperature is increased by 40.
  • We know that for every 10 degree rise in the temperature, the reverse saturation current double.
  • Determine the values at 40 degree centigrade.
  • The difference is 15 degree.
  • At 40 degree, what is the current?
  • We need to calculate the current in the forward bias condition if the forward bias is 0.2 at room temperature.
  • If the temperature is increased to 30 degree centigrade.
  • Therefore, VT is 0.8 and actual current calculation is 1.83 amps.
  • Find the current at 40 degree centigrade.
  • We use the whole formula last time what we used.
  • Substitute that and get the ID which is 281.49 milliamps.
  • Next, fourth, the reverse saturation current of germanium is two pico at 27 degree.
  • So we use the same principle concept where IS calculated first.
  • Substitute the value and calculate the reverse saturation current.
  • Determine the forward bias also.
  • The forward bias voltage VA.
